title: A partner page that is not a logo dump
metaTitle: Partner pages that say what you get
excerpt: A partner page should say what the customer gets from each relationship. Put that sentence beside the name, and skip logos that change nothing for the buyer.
alt: An open notebook with the word Notes underlined, a fountain pen, and glasses on a wooden desk, the page where a partnership is written as a sentence before it becomes a logo.
caption: Notes, a pen, and glasses. Write the partnership as a sentence first. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a partner page say under each logo?
faqs.answer: Say what changes for the customer because that partnership exists, in one sentence. Add the boundary, such as a country limit or a plan that does not include the connection. If you cannot write the sentence, leave the logo off the page.

faqs.question: Where should famous logos sit on the page?
faqs.answer: Group partners by the job a customer is trying to do, such as pay, ship, or sign in. Inside a group, put the option most people will use first. A famous mark helps only the visitor who came looking for that name.

faqs.question: When should a partner come off the page?
faqs.answer: Take the tile down in the same week the partnership or the connection ends. A dead integration is a support ticket printed on the marketing site. Keep the logo files with the rest of the brand so the next edit uses the right mark.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A partner page tells a customer what they get because you work with someone else. The partner's name is the proof. The sentence under it is the point. Partner page design starts with that sentence, then the mark, then a way to see the work when there is work to see.

Write the sentence before you collect logos. A visitor who does not already know the partner needs a reason to care. The page is for that visitor.

## The sentence each partner has to earn

Write one sentence before you export a file. The sentence answers a customer question: what changes for me because this partnership exists.

A payment partner shortens checkout or adds a card the buyer already holds. A shipping partner names the countries you reach and the window. A technology partner means a feature the buyer can turn on. A distribution partner means the product is stocked somewhere the buyer already goes. If you cannot finish the sentence, the tile is decoration.

Keep the sentence in the customer's language. "You can pay with the card you already use" is a reason to stay. "Orders land in the inbox your warehouse already checks" is a job. "Strategic alliance" is a line for a press note. Save it for the press note.

On a Hanabi project the sentence is drafted with the page. The layout can wait. A short list of honest sentences is more useful than a finished wall of marks with nothing under them. The studio designs and builds, so the sentence and the tile are one piece of work, not a design file waiting for someone else to invent the words.

Test the sentence on someone who does not work at the partner. If they can say what they would do next, the sentence is done. If they ask what the partnership is for, rewrite it. Do this before you argue about logo size.

Two sentences is the ceiling. The first is the job. The second is the boundary, covered below. A paragraph under every logo turns the page into a brochure. People will not read twenty brochures in a row.

## Why the first ten seconds need a sentence

People do not settle in to study a partner page. Nielsen Norman Group's article on how long people stay on web pages is plain about the opening. Users often leave in 10 to 20 seconds. To hold attention longer, the page has to communicate its value in about 10 seconds. The average visit lasts a little less than a minute, and people have time to read only about a quarter of the text on the pages they actually open.

A wall of marks spends those seconds on recognition. Recognition works for a logo the visitor already trusts. Everyone else sees a pattern of shapes. The page then loses the people who needed the sentence, which is most of them.

The same research describes a harsh first judgment. If the page survives about half a minute, people may stay much longer. You earn that stay by being clear early. A sentence under the first marks can do it. A preface that says you partner with industry leaders does not. The value has to sit with the partner it belongs to, where the eye lands.

Treat the hero the same way. One heading that names the job, then the first group. A carousel of greyscale marks hides the sentence. Leave the motion for something that explains a step.

## What sits next to the mark

Each entry needs four things. Keep to four if you want the page to stay readable.

The name, written out, so the mark is not the only way to read it. A logo is an image. The name is text a person can select and a search tool can read. Alt text on the image should be the partner's name, not "partner logo" twenty times.

The sentence, one line, about the customer. Leave out the history of how the deal was signed. Leave out the year unless the year changes the customer's decision, which it almost never does.

The boundary. What the partnership does not cover. A shipping mark does not mean you ship everywhere. A software mark does not mean every plan includes the connection. The boundary keeps the page from becoming a promise a support thread will have to undo.

A next step, when there is one. Link to the setup note, the country list, or the project where the partnership is visible. If there is no next step, skip the link. Sending the buyer to the partner's homepage hands them away at the moment they were deciding about you.

Use the same order every time. The eye learns the pattern on the first entry and applies it to the rest. One partner with a case study, the next with a tagline, and the third with a press quote is three layouts fighting.

## Order the page by the job

Group partners the way a customer looks for them. Pay. Ship. Sign in. Install. Refer. If you only have one group, say the job in the heading. "Partners" is a label. "Ways to pay" is a decision.

Inside a group, put the option most customers will use first. The rare enterprise connection can sit lower, with its own sentence, so it does not crowd the common path. A famous logo helps the visitor who came to check for that name. Everyone else needs the option they will actually touch.

If a partner exists only as a contract exhibit, leave them off the customer page. A journalist who needs the full list can have it in a press note. The customer page is the list a buyer can act on.

Two groups are enough for most companies. A third group is often a sign you are filing logos. Split when the jobs are truly different. Pay and ship are different. "Technology" and "platform" are often the same shelf with two headings.

Say how a customer chooses inside the group, in one line at the top of it. "Use this if your warehouse already runs on it" is a rule. A row of equal tiles with no rule asks the buyer to guess, and a guess is how the wrong integration gets promised on a sales call.

## Proof is a path, not a badge

A logo says a relationship exists. Proof is a customer seeing the relationship do something.

If the partnership changes checkout, show the step it changes. Down the Cove is a public Hanabi project, an ecommerce migration and redesign. The useful lesson for a partner page is the shopper's path. A strip of payment marks under a hero does less than one sentence about how an order is paid and where it goes. If you cannot show the path, do not imply a depth of integration you do not have.

Thomas Bewick, the editorial heritage site, is a different kind of public proof. A partner page for a publisher, a printer, or an archive would name what the partner does to the object. Who prints. Who distributes. Who keeps the record. The work itself is the evidence. The lockup is the label.

Write the proof in one or two sentences beside the mark, or link to a single project. A full case study for every partner turns the page into a maze. Longer stories belong with the work. The partner page carries the sentence and the pointer.

When you have no public story yet, say what the customer can do next. "Invoices export to the tool your bookkeeper already uses" is a job, even before you have a quotation from a client. Do not invent a quotation. A made-up line is worse than a plain sentence.

A partner tile should survive the same question a project has to survive: what was decided, and for whom?

## What to leave off the page

Leave off partners you are still negotiating. A tile with "coming soon" is a promise. If the integration slips, the page is what the buyer will cite.

Leave off the partner's slogan, their funding news, and their awards. None of that tells your customer what they get from you.

Leave off mutual marketing with no customer effect. A webinar from last spring can live on an events list. It does not earn a permanent tile.

Leave off marks you do not have the right to use at the size and color the page needs. A stretched logo, or a logo on a background the partner forbids, makes the relationship look careless. Get the files, or hold the tile.

Leave off a count in the hero. Ten partners with sentences beat a trophy number. If you truly have a directory a buyer must search, give them search, grouped by job. The count can sit in a quiet line if a salesperson needs it. It should not be the headline.

Also leave off the partner's entire product suite. You integrated one thing. Say that thing. Listing every product the partner sells implies you support all of it. Sales will spend the next quarter correcting the page.

## Keeping the page true

Name an owner inside your company. When a partnership ends, the tile comes down the same week. A dead integration is a support ticket you printed on the marketing site.

Review the sentences when the product changes. If the shipping window moved, the sentence is false. If a plan no longer includes the connection, the boundary is false. False is a more serious problem than a dated layout.

Keep the files with the rest of the brand, where the next person can find them. On a Hanabi project that place is the client portal, with the other brand files, docs, and updates after delivery. A logo folder in a chat thread is how the next redesign ships the wrong color version.

The page should still look like your site. Same type. Same link style. You can give the marks room to breathe. You do not need a separate visual language for them. Hanabi builds these pages in the same system as the rest of the site, usually Next.js, React, and TypeScript, with type and color from the brand already in Figma. A partner page that suddenly becomes a dark showcase is a second site.

When the sentences are true, compare the page with work that gives each project a job. [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is that comparison: a frame earns its place by the decision it shows. Read your partner tiles the same way. If a mark needs a caption to make sense, write the caption.

A short promotion is a different problem. It needs an end date, and it can be louder than the homepage while using the same type and the same offer. The piece on [seasonal campaigns that stay inside the brand](/blog/seasonal-campaigns-without-a-new-brand) is the next read if your "partner" is actually a month of attention.
